scene.testo: Four people, one capsule, and a ride that tops 17,000 miles per hour in just twelve minutes. Inside the SpaceX Dragon, you go from sitting on a pad to floating weightless, faster than any airliner could ever dream.
But how do four humans live inside a cabin smaller than a minivan? Where do they sit, sleep, eat, and even use the toilet? And what happens when something goes wrong?
The scariest part is not the launch. It is a seven-minute blackout during reentry, when nobody on Earth can talk to you. Stay with me, because we are going inside Dragon, step by step.

First, meet the machine. Dragon began as a cargo ship. Its first version started flying to the International Space Station in 2010, and it completed 23 cargo missions before SpaceX built a version for people.

NASA backed the crew version through its Commercial Crew Program. The first crewed flight launched on May 30, 2020. It was the first American crewed spacecraft to reach orbit since the Space Shuttle retired in 2011.

The capsule itself stands about sixteen feet tall and thirteen feet wide. Underneath sits the trunk, adding roughly twelve more feet. Together, that is taller than a basketball hoop is high, stacked more than once.
The trunk is more than a tail. It carries unpressurized cargo, and it holds the solar panels that power the spacecraft. Before reentry, it gets cut loose and burns up, so only the capsule comes home.
At the very front, a hinged nose cone swings open. Behind it hides a docking port for trips to the station. On free-flying missions, that spot can carry a glass dome instead.
Dragon uses two kinds of thrusters. Sixteen small Draco engines steer the capsule and adjust its orbit. They burn two chemicals that ignite on contact, so there is no spark plug, no fuss, just fire.
Then come the SuperDracos, eight larger engines hidden in four pods around the capsule. Each one delivers about sixteen thousand pounds of thrust. They exist for one reason: to save your life.
If the rocket fails during ascent, those engines fire in about a tenth of a second and fling the capsule away from the booster. In seven seconds, Dragon covers roughly half a mile.
Those fins on the trunk look pointless in space, and they are. They are there to keep Dragon stable if it ever has to fly through air alone during an emergency escape from the rocket.
Now step inside. The pressurized cabin holds about 330 cubic feet, enough for four people. For comparison, Russia's Soyuz descent module offers roughly 140 cubic feet, and it is designed for three.

Picture the old Apollo cockpit: hundreds of switches, dials, and lights. Now picture Dragon instead. In front of the crew, there are three large touchscreens. That is the cockpit. It feels more like a tablet than a spaceship.

Dragon flies itself. Astronauts can monitor and give commands, but ground teams in Hawthorne, California, can handle much of the work remotely. For a crew, that means less button pushing and more looking out the window.

Compare that with Boeing's Starliner, which still has physical switches and controls. Dragon's clean, screen-based design is a real break from decades of spacecraft cockpits packed with analog hardware.

Now it is launch day, and you need a suit. Each astronaut gets a custom-fitted pressure suit and a 3D-printed helmet. It looks sleek, but its job is deadly serious: keeping you alive if the cabin loses pressure.

Without pressure, water boils at a far lower temperature, and body fluids can start to vaporize. The suit holds sea-level-style pressure around you. Ideally, nobody ever needs it, like a seatbelt you hope never matters.
The suit is a single piece. You step in through the waist and zip up. Communications and health monitoring are built in, and the helmet seals the system, so everything you need is wrapped around you.
About three hours before liftoff, the crew suits up at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. They get a final briefing, then head out for a ride that is surprisingly familiar: an electric Tesla Model X.
The Tesla carries the crew to the launch pad. Its gull-wing doors make it easier to climb in and out while wearing a bulky suit, which is exactly why this odd choice actually makes sense.
At the pad, an elevator lifts the crew about 255 feet to the crew access arm. That is roughly a twenty-story building. Up there, a landline phone waits for any last words to family and friends.

Then comes the short walk across the access arm to the hatch. Ground crews help each astronaut squeeze in, strap down, and connect to the seat. This is the last time you touch anything solid on Earth.
Your boots clip into the floor so your legs stay put. A hose from the seat plugs into your suit, flowing cooled air and oxygen. At that moment, you and Dragon become one connected system.

About forty-five minutes before launch, the ground crew says goodbye and closes the hatch. The access arm swings away. Visors come down. You hear nothing now except fans, valves, and your own breathing.
Next, the crew arms the launch escape system. It is one of the few jobs done from inside the capsule. A loud bang follows as the SuperDraco fuel tanks are pressurized. Not exactly calming.

Then fueling begins, with you already aboard. SpaceX loads the Falcon 9 with crew inside, a procedure unusual in human spaceflight. You can hear valves opening and super-cold propellant rushing through the rocket below.

On your three screens, live data scrolls by, much like the SpaceX webcast viewers watch at home, with extra technical detail. The final minutes arrive. You grip nothing, because there is nothing to grip.

Ignition. Nine Merlin engines at the base of the Falcon 9 booster generate about 1.7 million pounds of thrust. The whole stack shakes, then climbs. Within seconds, you are pressed hard into your seat.

Around the one-minute mark, the rocket passes the speed of sound. Then comes the highest-stress phase of ascent, called max Q, when aerodynamic pressure peaks. The ride is loud, rough, and fast, then it smooths out.

At about two minutes and thirty seconds, the first-stage engines shut down and the stage separates. You are already traveling several thousand miles per hour, more than fifty miles up. The upper stage takes over.
Around nine minutes after liftoff, the second engine cuts off. You are near 17,000 miles per hour at about 125 miles of altitude. Suddenly the shaking stops, and anything loose begins to float.
Crews often bring a small plush toy as a zero-gravity indicator. When it lifts off the floor and drifts in front of the cameras, everyone knows without a word: you have arrived in space.

About twelve minutes in, Dragon separates from the second stage and begins flying on its own. Fifteen minutes in, you can lift your visor and unstrap. You float free inside the capsule for the first time.
From here, your trip splits in two. If you are heading to the International Space Station, Dragon spends roughly a day chasing it. Slowly, carefully, it raises and matches its orbit until docking.

For station missions, the nose cone opens and exposes the docking port. Dragon connects automatically, and the crew floats through the hatch to join the station residents. A long stay awaits them there.
The other kind of trip is a private flight, like Inspiration4, which stayed in low Earth orbit for about three days. No station, no docking port. Instead, a glass dome replaces the nose cone.
Inside that dome, you can put your whole head and see Earth all around you at once. Sunrises come every ninety minutes or so. Many astronauts have described that view as unforgettable.
Sooner or later, someone has to use the toilet. In Mercury, Alan Shepard famously had to wait on the pad and ended up relieving himself in his suit. Space plumbing has come a long way since May 1961.
Today, a vacuum toilet pulls waste away with airflow instead of gravity. Dragon has one above the side hatch. It is tucked in a wall compartment with fans, hoses, and storage, plus a privacy curtain.

Weightlessness changes how the body works, and the urge can arrive fast. Crews have reported that nearly everyone ends up using the toilet within hours of reaching orbit. So no, you cannot just hold it.
Now it is time to come home. Flight controllers pick one of seven landing zones off the Florida coast, in the Atlantic or the Gulf of Mexico, depending on weather and sea conditions on the day.

Dragon lowers its orbit step by step. Then the trunk separates, and Draco thrusters point the heat shield forward. The crew puts suits back on, lowers visors, and braces for the most violent part of the trip.

Dragon slams into the atmosphere at about 17,500 miles per hour. Air compresses and glows as superheated plasma, around 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit outside, roughly 1,900 degrees Celsius. Communications drop out for about seven minutes.

The heat shield is ablative. Its outer layer burns away on purpose, carrying the heat with it. Inside, cooled air flows through your suit, and the crew feels roughly four to five times Earth's gravity.
Then drogue parachutes open, followed by four main parachutes, slowing Dragon to about fifteen miles per hour at touchdown. Splash. You are floating in the ocean, bobbing, and finally safe.

Recovery crews arrive fast, but first they must cover the thrusters. The leftover fuel is toxic, so teams wear breathing masks. Then a crane lifts the capsule aboard the ship. The white paint now looks charred.

The hatch opens. Crews have to climb and slide out, since gravity suddenly weighs a lot. After a long stay in orbit, walking can be hard, and doctors often help. The surprise: Dragon gets refurbished and flies again.

descrizione:
What is it really like to ride inside the SpaceX Dragon capsule? In this Orbital Days documentary, we follow a crew from suit-up and the Tesla ride to launch, orbit, the space toilet, reentry at about 17,500 mph, and splashdown. We cover the Crew Dragon cabin, SuperDraco abort engines, the heat shield, and how private flights differ from International Space Station trips, using only documented facts from NASA and SpaceX.

You will learn how big the cabin really is, how astronauts get strapped in, what the three touchscreens do, why the capsule has fins, and what happens during the seven-minute communications blackout on the way home.

Subscribe to Orbital Days for more journeys into real life in space, every week.
